messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

output:
## About

We build scheduling software for medical clinics. That is the whole company.

Meridian started in 2017 in a two-doctor family practice in Bend, Oregon, where our founder was working as a practice manager and rebuilding the next day's schedule by hand every evening. Three no-shows, one provider out sick, a double-booked ultrasound room. The software the clinic already owned could store appointments. It could not help her put them back together.

So the first version of Meridian did one thing: it took the day apart and proposed a new version of it, with the constraints a clinic actually has. Provider licensure. Room and equipment conflicts. The rule that a Medicaid follow-up cannot be pushed past a certain window. Interpreter availability, which almost no scheduling tool models at all.

Today about 1,400 clinics use us, most of them independent practices between two and forty providers. Median no-show rate among our customers dropped from 14% to 9% in the first year on the product; we publish the methodology behind that number on our metrics page, including the clinics where it did not move.

We are 31 people, remote across the US and Canada, with roughly a third of the team having worked in a clinic before working here. We are profitable and have taken no outside investment, which means we answer to the practices paying us rather than to a return schedule.

We are not trying to become your EHR. We integrate with the one you have, and we would rather be the small piece of your day that stops being a problem.
